text.text:
### Prerequisites

In this text, we will continue exploring the idea of equality: we will compare how different cultures understand the "world". For a more detailed understanding, we recommend studying the previous texts on comparisons in the "First steps" section (<htcite0>).

### Introduction

In the previous text, we learned that calendars, in general, count the number of days that pass from a starting point. Although they share the same idea, different cultures created calendars in different ways (<htcite0>).

This fact, related to time, leads us to a reflection:

Reflection 1: Is it only about time?

If people from different cultures had different understandings of how to count time, could they also have had different understandings of other things, such as the idea of world?

### A local view

To better understand how the "world" was understood in antiquity, we need to look at the period in which those people lived and at how they described their world. This way, we avoid mistaken generalizations.

#### A Mesoamerican case

In the year <htdate0>, the city of Copán was conquered by the same general who conquered Tikal: Sihyaj K’ahk’, who had ties to Teotihuacan, located in central Mexico (<htcite0>; <htcite1>). From this fact, we can conclude that they had at least heard of the region.

On the other hand, when we look at the inscription on Stela A (Figure 1), written in the times of Waxaklajuun Ubaah K’awiil — also known as 18 Rabbit — and made before <htdate1>, the year of his death (<htcite2>), we see that the conquerors are not mentioned in its description. At that time, only four great urban centers are mentioned — Copán, Tikal, Calakmul, and Palenque — which represent the cardinal points (<htcite3>; <htcite4>).

Figure 1: Stela A in the Museum of the Archaeological Site of Copán. It mentions the cities of Copán, Tikal, Calakmul, and Palenque, in this order (). The photo was taken in , during a visit to the site.

source.text: Instituto Hondureño de Antropologia e Historia

text.imgdesc: In this image, there is a hieroglyphic text arranged in two columns.

text.text: The absence of any mention of cities outside the Maya world leads us to a reflection:

Reflection 2: A new horizon

At that moment, the world of Copán no longer had Teotihuacan on its horizon, because that city had lost the dominance of earlier times.

Would it make sense for them to cite it?

Does the local world turn what exists around it into something nonexistent?

Based on this reflection, we can conclude that the relevance of the four great centers appears precisely because they are cited. This relevance, however, does not erase the existence of earlier cities or of cities contemporary with them.

### The Roman world

Since Stela A (Figure 1) was written after the fall of the Western Roman Empire, in the year <htdate0> (<htcite0>), we cannot use it for a direct comparison with texts from that empire. That is why we will turn to a city contemporary with the Roman Empire: Teotihuacan (Figure 2).
Figure 2: General view of Teotihuacan. The photo was taken in , during a visit to the site.
text.imgdesc: General view of the city of Teotihuacan. In the image, we can see several buildings in the talud-tablero style and, in the background, two pyramidal structures that represent sacred mountains.

text.text:
#### The size of Teotihuacan

Teotihuacan's victory over Tikal (Guatemala) and the influence that reached as far as Copán (Honduras) did not happen by chance.

Archaeological excavations show that the city was inhabited between <htdate0> and <htdate1>. At its height (<htdate2> - <htdate3>), Teotihuacan had as many as 100,000 inhabitants, making it the sixth largest city in the world, behind places such as Rome, Constantinople, and Alexandria (<htcite0>).

Reflection 3: As big as Rome?

Given the importance Teotihuacan had in its own time, and the fact that it was contemporary with the Roman Empire, can we conclude that Rome mentioned the city in some way?

#### The Roman view

When we examine Speech 26, by Aelius Aristides, addressed to Rome in the second century of the Gregorian calendar, we find a much broader view of what was meant by the "inhabited world". Below, we highlight some of the places mentioned — the numbers indicate the paragraphs of the speech (<htcite0>):
- **6**: Argos, in present-day Greece
- **8**: "Italy... as far as the Strait of Otranto", the strait between Italy and Albania (<htcite1>).
- **9**: Athens and Laconia, both in Greece.
- **10**: Asia, Africa, and Europe are mentioned, without stating the known limits of the continents. Chelidonian and Cyanean are also mentioned as the frontier of the empire in Anatolia, in present-day Turkey.
- **12**: India and Arabia are mentioned, as well as Greek regions such as Naxos, in Sicily (<htcite2>), Cythnos, and Athens. Finally, estates in Egypt and Sicily are mentioned, and part of Africa is classified as civilized.
- **13**: The Roman understanding of the world becomes clear in this passage of the speech: "..and as Hesiod mentioned about the end of the Ocean, there is a common channel where all waters have a single origin and destination, therefore there is a channel common to Rome and they all gather here."
- **15**: The Persian Empire is mentioned, along with its relationship with the Hellenes (Greeks).
- **16**: The Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea are mentioned.
- **17**: Further mentions of regions such as Ionia, the western coast of Anatolia, in present-day Turkey (<htcite3>), and Lydia, in Turkey. In addition to these regions, we also highlight the mention of a region beyond the Euphrates.
- **18**: Continuing with regions of Mesopotamia and beyond, we find mentions of the emperor Cyrus, as well as Babylon, Susa, and Ecbatana, the latter two in present-day Iran (<htcite4>; <htcite5>).
- **22 and 23**: Further mentions of the Persian Empire.
- **24 - 27**: Mentions of Alexander and his conquests. In one of them, it is said that he "advanced over the greater part of the earth". At the end, it is mentioned that the Macedonian empire was divided after his death.
- **28**: When mentioning the extent the empire reached, he cites the Red Sea, the cataracts of the Nile, and the Sea of Azov. Another point worth highlighting in his speech is the fact that some writers "did not believe that the ocean existed".
- **31**: Once again, there is a mention of a "civilized world".
- **36**: Mention of Caria and Phrygia, in present-day Turkey (<htcite6>), and of Egypt.
- **42 - 59**: Description of the Hellenic states.
- **60**: There is a description of the Roman Empire that we wish to highlight: "Neither the sea nor the continent that lies between them constitute barriers to citizenship, nor do Asia and Europe receive different treatment here. In this empire, all roads are open to all".
- **63**: Still about the peoples around the Roman world, we find this remark: "For the categories by which you now divide the world are not Hellenes and barbarians — and the distinction you have made is not absurd, since you offer them a citizenship more numerous, so to speak, than the entire Hellenic race. The division you have adopted instead is between Romans and non-Romans. To such a degree have you expanded the name of your city."
- **73 - 74**: Greeks and Egyptians are mentioned.
- **82**: The region of Aethiopia is mentioned alongside Phasis, a region near the Black Sea.
- **85 - 86**: Persians and Egyptians are mentioned.
- **91**: A mention of the process of slavery: "The Macedonians knew slavery under the Persians; the Persians, under the Medes; the Medes, under the Assyrians; but, since men have had knowledge of you, all have known you as rulers."
- **101**: A phrase of Homer is recalled: "Earth common for all".

Despite the use of the words "Earth" and also "world", the analysis of the places mentioned in the speech shows no kind of knowledge associated with the peoples who lived in America (*Abya Yala*). Furthermore, we stress that Aelius Aristides himself mentions that some writers did not know about the ocean. To make even clearer the regions mentioned by Aelius Aristides in his speech, in Figure 3 we highlight these regions by overlaying them on the current world map as follows: - Roman Empire : Approximate region of the Roman Empire in the year 117 (), a date close to when Aelius Aristides wrote his speech. - Persians : Aelius Aristides mentions the Persians who, in his time, were rivals of Rome, but no longer formed the same Achaemenid Empire. During his lifetime, the Parthians were their neighbors (). - Arabia : The mention of Arabia in the speech possibly referred to the Roman province (). Although nations today use this name, we should not confuse them with that province. - Aethiopia : The region of Aethiopia cannot be clearly defined; therefore, we mark it on the map in an illustrative way only. It could range from a state south of Egypt that even inflicted a defeat on Rome, to a more general way of referring to Black Africans, which would greatly expand the region defined as Aethiopia (). - India : India is another region we cannot clearly mark, because, in the times when the speech was written, the region was divided among different empires and kings (). In this way, we paint the entire ancient region in generic terms. - Seas mentioned : Regarding the seas mentioned, we should stress that they are only a small part of all the non-continental area we know of today.

source.text: Singh, R. P. B., & Rana, P. S.

text.text: Figure 3: Approximate map of the Roman world painted over the currently known world map. © Mapswire ().
Considering that Aelius Aristides had much more knowledge than the general population of the Roman Empire, let us take a new reflection:

Reflection 4: If those who know do not know, who does not know...?

Aelius Aristides mentions an earth and a world that are not the earth and the world we know today. Even so, his description of the Roman world is quite broad.

If he, with all the studies and information he had, did not know the world as we know it, could someone inside the empire, without the same access to that knowledge, have had an idea of the world as we know it today?

Suppose that, for some reason, you conclude that the answer is yes: what archaeological evidence would you use to prove it?

### A Babylonian view

Since human knowledge grows over time, we should expect that the further back we go, the more restricted the view of the world we will find.

A good example of this appears when we examine the earliest map we know of, made in Babylon (Figure 4).
Figure 4: Map of the "world" © Trustees of the British Museum ().
text.imgdesc: In this figure, there is a clay tablet with inscriptions. On it, we see a large central circle, with triangles on its outer edge.

text.text: This map, from Babylon, shows that, in their understanding, the world was limited to nearby lands — with no mention of other continents or seas (<htcite0>; <htcite1>). This is quite different from what we understand today as planet Earth (<htcite2>; <htcite3>).

source.text: Hu, X., Shum, C.K. & Bevis, M

text.text: To make the regions represented by the Babylonian map more evident, compared with what we know of our world today, we follow the explanation of Dr. Irving Finkel (<htcite0>) and overlay the Babylonian map on the current world map (Figure 5).

Figure 5: Map of the Babylonian world © Trustees of the British Museum () overlaid on the current world map © Mapswire (). Shared under the license Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).
text.imgdesc: In this image, we can see that the ancient Babylonian map covers an extremely small area compared with the world we know today.

text.text:
### Toward the present

So far, we have seen how, in remote times, different peoples made local descriptions: when they spoke of "world", they referred only to their own world — the peoples they lived with and the limits they knew. We have not yet addressed, however, the scenario in which we begin to speak of the world we know today, with its different continents. In this section, we will deal with the encounter between Europeans and Chinese.

#### Matteo Ricci's representation

When Europeans set out to sea in order to find new routes to the Indies, it was not only their navigation specialists who embarked. Some religious figures accompanied them as well, among them the Jesuit Matteo Ricci, who made the map in Figure 6. As can be seen on the map, the Jesuit represented his understanding of the world in the seventeenth century, according to the Gregorian calendar, with China (Zhongguo 中國) at the center, holding a relevance analogous to that of Europe (<htcite0>).
Figure 6: Map by Matteo Ricci, in which the continent is highlighted ().

Although this map does not exactly represent the world we know today, among all those we have seen so far, it is the one that comes closest to our current understanding of the world as a whole. Even so, Matteo Ricci's work lacked an understanding of equality for our entire species.

### Conclusion

In this text, we saw descriptions of the world made by different peoples (Maya, Romans, Babylonians, Chinese, and Europeans). None of the descriptions we analyzed reflects what we know about our world today, even though, in the times of the Roman Empire, the description used words such as "earth" and "world".

Simply saying that they were wrong may lead us to make a mistake of our own. What we saw in this text, in fact, shows that words change meaning over time: it is not enough to read a text, we must also study the words and the period in which the authors lived, in order to truly understand what they meant to say.

exercise_v2.question: Has humanity always understood the Earth as having its current shape and described it exactly as we know it today?
exercise_v2.additionalInfo: Our knowledge of the Earth — and of nature as a whole — has grown over time. Ancient texts, maps, and stelae show that descriptions of places did not necessarily reflect the world we know today, even though some peoples called the region they knew "the world".

exercise_v2.question: In the speech we studied about the Roman Empire, is it clear that the Romans knew Teotihuacan?
exercise_v2.additionalInfo: Nowhere in the text we studied is there any mention of the peoples who lived in America (Abya Yala). Moreover, there is no archaeological find that would allow us to suppose that the Romans and those peoples ever came into contact with one another.
